Swap the brain

Think of a game console: the console never changes, you swap the cartridge.

  • The console is one network, written once into the CSS. It knows the rules of tic-tac-toe, but it has no strategy of its own.
  • The cartridge is a strategy, and a strategy is just a list of 1,801 numbers. The three buttons swap cartridges.
  • Try: pick Random and win easily. Pick Hand-written: it wins and blocks, but you can trap it. Pick Trained: you can't beat it. Same console every time; only the numbers changed.
Small numbers: how much the strategy liked each square.

How it works (for the curious)

The models

Model
Trainedthe tic-tac-toe demo's network, trained on every position
Hand-written48 hand-set hidden units: win if you can, else block, else centre, corner, edge
Randomuntrained: random int8 weights

Each one is an 18 → 64 → 9 network with int8 weights. The page keeps them as three CSS rules of 1,801 numbers each and nothing else. Change the numbers and the same interpreter plays something else.

The hard part: multiplying

To use the cartridge, the console has to multiply its numbers, but a network can't multiply two of its inputs, only add them up. So it splits each number into pieces, like 5 = 4 + 1, and turns 5 × 7 into 4 × 7 + 1 × 7: just adding.

A ReLU network can only add up its inputs with fixed weights, and here the model's weights are inputs too. So every weight × activation is built from ReLUs. The weights come in as unsigned bytes u = w + 128.

Checked in numpy: for all three models, on every position and every X move (25,893 cases), the interpreter's logits and move equal the model's own forward pass. It is also exact on 300 random models with weights at the edges of the int8 range; those can push sums past 2²⁴, so the page only loads models that are checked to stay under it. The browser test plays each model's games in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit.
